title: The charge ladder: which materials give electrons, which take them, and where the charge goes

summary.text: A plain hand pulls a charged balloon, and so does a charged ruler. So how can you tell which one is really charged? Only a push proves it. In this unit you rub six materials on wool and on polythene, and use the pushes to build a ladder of who gives electrons and who takes them. A material in the middle gives to the rungs below it and takes from the rungs above it. So plus and minus describe how two things meet, not what one thing is. You also follow the charge as it runs through metal and a body into the Earth, and find out why that matters in a printing press, a petrol tanker and a storm.
summary.art: A balloon hanging on a thread between a child's open hand on one side and a rubbed ruler on the other, the balloon leaning towards the hand and swinging away from the ruler.

intro.hook: Rub a balloon on your hair and hang it from a thread. Hold your open hand near it. The balloon swings towards your hand. Now hold a ruler you rubbed on wool near it. The balloon swings away. One thing pulled and one thing pushed. Which of them proves that something is charged?
intro.text: Your hand has no extra charge, yet it pulled the balloon. The ruler pushed, and a push needs charge on both sides. In this unit you use pushes to find out which materials give away electrons and which take them. You hang a foil ball that changes its mind, peel tape into twins, and build a ladder from your own results. Then you follow the charge as it runs away through a steel spoon or a hand, and find out why a printing press in Sivakasi and a petrol tanker both need that to happen.
intro.art: A balloon on a thread between a plain hand and a rubbed plastic ruler, with a small arrow towards the hand and a small arrow away from the ruler.

outcomes: I can say that rubbing only moves electrons from one thing to another, so one thing gains exactly what the other loses.
I can explain why only a push, not a pull, proves that a thing is charged.
I can rank materials by which takes electrons and which gives them, and use my ladder to predict a pair I have not tried.
I can explain why a material in the middle of the ladder can give electrons to one partner and take them from another.
I can explain how charge runs through conductors, stays on insulators, and is carried away by earthing, damp air or a sharp point.
I can explain that the push between charges gets weaker quickly with distance and stronger with more charge.
I can explain how a spark and lightning happen, and why static helps in a printer and is dangerous near fuel and dust.
I can say what scientists still do not know about how rubbing moves charge.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle with a minus charge that moves around the middle of an atom. Electrons are the charges that move when you rub things.
terms.example: When a balloon is rubbed on wool, electrons move from the wool to the balloon.
terms.art: An atom with a plus centre and three small minus dots circling it, and one dot leaving.

terms.meaning: The two kinds of electric charge. Two of the same kind push apart. One of each kind pull together.
terms.example: A balloon rubbed on wool has extra minus charge, so it pushes away another rubbed balloon.
terms.art: Two small circles marked with a plus and a minus, with arrows pulling them together, and two circles both marked minus, with arrows pushing them apart.

terms.meaning: Having equal plus and minus charge, so there is no extra charge to feel from far away.
terms.example: A plain steel spoon is neutral until something gives it or takes from it a charge.
terms.art: A spoon with the same number of small plus and minus marks all over it.

terms.meaning: Charge is never made or destroyed. It only moves from one place to another, so what one thing gains, another loses.
terms.example: If the balloon gains a million electrons from the wool, the wool loses exactly a million.
terms.art: Two cloths side by side with the same number of small dots moving from one to the other.

terms.meaning: Charge moving between two materials when they touch and then come apart. Rubbing helps because it makes more touching.
terms.example: Clear tape pulled off a table leaves both the tape and the table with a charge.
terms.art: A strip of clear tape being peeled off a table, with tiny plus and minus marks on the tape and the table.

terms.meaning: A list of materials in order. A material higher on the ladder gives electrons to one lower down. The scientific name is the triboelectric series.
terms.example: On most ladders wool is near the top and polythene is near the bottom, so wool gives electrons to polythene.
terms.art: A ladder with wool at the top, paper and cotton in the middle, and polythene at the bottom, and an arrow down the side labelled electrons go this way.

terms.meaning: To push away. Only two things with the same kind of charge repel each other.
terms.example: Two balloons rubbed on hair hang apart in a V, because they repel.
terms.art: Two balloons hanging from one point on threads, swung apart in a V shape.

terms.meaning: When a charged thing comes near a neutral one, the neutral thing's plus and minus charges shift a little, so the near side has the opposite charge. This is why a charged thing can pull a neutral one.
terms.example: A rubbed balloon pulls a bit of paper, even though the paper has no extra charge.
terms.art: A minus balloon near a paper bit, with the paper's near side marked plus and its far side marked minus.

terms.meaning: A material that lets charge move through it easily.
terms.example: A steel spoon is a conductor, so a charge on it runs away into your hand.
terms.art: A steel spoon with small arrows showing dots running along it into a hand.

terms.meaning: A material that does not let charge move through it easily, so charge stays where it was put.
terms.example: A plastic spoon is an insulator, so a charge on it stays put.
terms.art: A plastic spoon with small minus marks sitting still on its surface.

terms.meaning: Joining something to the ground with a conductor, so any extra charge can flow away into the huge Earth.
terms.example: Many petrol tankers trail a metal chain or strap on the road, and at the fuel depot they are clipped to a metal earth wire, so charge can drain into the ground.
terms.art: A petrol tanker with a metal chain hanging from it and touching the road.

terms.meaning: When extra charge leaves a charged thing, slowly through the air or a conductor, or suddenly as a spark.
terms.example: A charged foil ball discharges when you touch it with your finger.
terms.art: A foil ball on a thread with a finger touching it, and small dots flowing away along the finger.

terms.meaning: A sudden jump of charge through air, which glows and crackles because the air along the path is heated.
terms.example: A tiny spark may jump from your finger to a metal door handle on a dry day.
terms.art: A finger near a metal door handle with a small bright zigzag between them.

terms.meaning: A unit for how strongly charge is pushed to move. A bigger number of volts can push a spark across a bigger gap of air.
terms.example: A torch cell is 1.5 volts. A spark you can feel needs about 3,000 volts.
terms.art: A small cell marked 1.5 volts next to a tall bar marked 3,000 volts.

terms.meaning: The space around a charge where another charge feels a push or a pull.
terms.example: A rubbed balloon has an electric field, so it can lift your arm hairs without touching them.
terms.art: A balloon with faint curved lines spreading out from it and lifting fine arm hairs.

terms.meaning: An atom or a piece of a molecule that has gained or lost electrons, so it carries a charge.
terms.example: Salt in water splits into ions, which is why salty water carries charge.
terms.art: A grain of salt dissolving in a glass, with small plus and minus ions floating in the water.

explanations.concept: Rubbing moves electrons, and charge is never made
explanations.definition: Rubbing, or touching and pulling apart, moves electrons from one material to another. The total charge stays the same, so one material gains exactly what the other loses.
explanations.description: Every atom has a plus centre, made of protons, and minus electrons around it. The protons are locked in the middle of the atom and stay put. Some electrons on the outside can be moved. When two different materials touch and come apart, some electrons stay with one and are left behind by the other. Now one has extra minus charge, and the other has missing minus, which acts like extra plus. Nothing was made. Charge only moved. Michael Faraday showed in 1843 that the two charges always come in equal pairs, by catching a charged thing inside a metal pail and measuring.
examples: A balloon rubbed on hair takes electrons from the hair, so the balloon is minus and the hair is plus.
Clear tape peeled off a table leaves one side of the pair minus and the other plus, in equal amounts.
A comb that pulls paper has taken or given a tiny fraction of its electrons, not made new ones.
explanations.art: A balloon and a hair strand side by side with the same number of small dots drawn moving from the hair to the balloon.

explanations.concept: Only a push proves a thing is charged
explanations.definition: Two charged things with the same kind of charge repel. A pull can come from a charge on one thing and nothing on the other, so only repelling shows that both are charged the same way.
explanations.description: A charged balloon pulls on a plain, neutral hand or wall. That surprises people. The balloon's charge shifts the neutral thing's own plus and minus charges a little, so the near side gets the opposite charge and the pull wins slightly. This is called polarisation. So a pull cannot tell you if the other thing is charged. A push can. The only way to push a minus balloon away is with another minus charge. That is why a scientist who wants to test a charge looks for repelling, and why the tests in this unit all watch for a push.
examples: A rubbed balloon swings towards a plain hand, so the pull does not prove the hand is charged.
A rubbed balloon swings away from a ruler rubbed on wool, so both have the same kind of charge.
A bit of paper jumps to a comb because of polarisation, not because the paper is charged.
explanations.art: A minus balloon with an arrow pulling a neutral hand towards it, and beside it the same balloon with an arrow pushing a minus ruler away.

explanations.definition: A charge ladder lists materials in order. When two are rubbed together, the one higher up gives electrons and the one lower down takes them. Its scientific name is the triboelectric series.
explanations.description: If you rub many pairs of materials and note who gets the minus charge each time, an order appears. Wool and hair are near the top. They give electrons to almost everything. Polythene, PVC and Teflon are near the bottom, and take electrons from almost everything. Paper and cotton are in the middle, and charge weakly with each other. The ladder lets you predict a pair you have never tried: whichever is lower gets the minus. Published ladders agree about the top and the bottom. They disagree about neighbours, and the order shifts with dryness, how clean the surface is and how hard you rub. So a ladder is a good guide for far-apart materials, and a poor one for close neighbours.
examples: Wool rubbed on polythene: wool is higher, so polythene gets the minus.
Cotton rubbed on a plastic ruler: cotton is higher, so the ruler gets the minus.
Paper rubbed on cotton: they are neighbours, so the charge is weak and the answer unreliable.
explanations.art: A ladder with twelve rungs from human hair at the top to PVC at the bottom, with an arrow along the side showing electrons moving down.

explanations.concept: A material in the middle both gives and takes
explanations.definition: On a ladder, a material gives electrons to every rung below it and takes electrons from every rung above it. Plus and minus therefore depend on the partner, not only on the material.
explanations.description: Take cotton. Rub it with wool, and wool is higher, so the cotton takes electrons and becomes minus. Rub the same cotton with polythene, and polythene is lower, so the cotton gives electrons and becomes plus. The cotton did not change. Its partner did. So you cannot call cotton a plus material or a minus material. You can only say what it does against a partner. Only the two ends of the ladder always do the same: the top gives and the bottom takes. Everything between is both, depending on who it meets.
examples: Cotton is minus against wool and plus against polythene.
Paper is minus against hair and plus against PVC.
Wool is plus against nearly everything, because it sits near the top.
explanations.art: Three cloths in a column, wool at the top, cotton in the middle and polythene at the bottom, with arrows showing electrons going from wool to cotton and from cotton to polythene.

explanations.concept: Plus and minus are names chosen before electrons were found
explanations.definition: The names plus and minus were chosen in the 1700s. Later, electrons were found to be the particles that move, and they carry the charge called minus.
explanations.description: Charles du Fay, in Paris in 1733, found that there are two kinds of charge. Benjamin Franklin, in 1747, said there is one electric fluid, and a thing has either too much of it or too little. He guessed that glass rubbed with silk gets too much, so he called its charge plus. In 1897 J. J. Thomson in Cambridge found the electron, a small particle that carries the charge now called minus. Glass rubbed with silk actually loses electrons, so Franklin had it backwards. The names stayed, because they work in the sums. So an electron has a minus charge only because of a guess made 150 years before it was found.
examples: Glass rubbed with silk loses electrons, so it is plus.
A balloon rubbed on hair gains electrons, so it is minus.
Moving electrons are minus charges, even though the name was chosen by guessing.
explanations.art: A portrait-style drawing of a man in 1700s clothes holding a glass rod and a silk cloth, with a small question mark over the rod.

explanations.concept: Why does rubbing move charge? Scientists still argue
explanations.description: Everyone agrees that touching two materials and pulling them apart can move charge. Nobody agrees yet on exactly what moves, or why one material wins over another. Even the same material can charge itself: in 2011 a team led by Bartosz Grzybowski found that one piece of plastic can have patches of plus and minus on its own surface, like a mosaic. And in 2014 researchers found that small and large grains of the very same material charged each other, with the larger grains usually ending up plus. A simple ladder cannot explain that.
examples: Clear tape peeled from the same roll has plus and minus patches.
Small and large grains of one material can charge each other.
Water on a surface can change the charge a material takes.
explanations.art: A close-up of a plastic surface drawn as a patchwork of small squares, some marked plus and some marked minus.

perspectives.explanation: Materials hold their outer electrons with different strengths. When two touch, electrons move from the one that holds them loosely to the one that holds them more strongly.

Thin films of water on every surface carry ions. These ions may move from one surface to the other, and the surface that gains the ions gets the charge. This view explains why humidity changes results so much.
Tiny bits of one material may be torn off and stick to the other, carrying their charge with them. Some measurements show this happening. In other measurements it does not.

explanations.concept: Conductors carry charge away, insulators keep it
explanations.definition: A conductor lets charge move through it freely. An insulator holds charge where it is.
explanations.description: Metals have outer electrons that are free to drift from atom to atom, so a charge put on one end of a steel spoon spreads out and runs into whatever touches it. Plastic, dry wood, glass and rubber hold their electrons tightly, so a charge put on one spot stays there. Your body is a conductor, because it is full of salty water. That is why you cannot charge a steel spoon by rubbing it while holding it in your hand. The charge runs through you to the floor. It is also why a charged plastic ruler loses its charge when you touch it with a wet finger.
examples: A steel spoon held in the hand cannot stay charged.
A plastic comb keeps its charge for a minute or more on a dry day.
A wet finger removes a charge in an instant.
explanations.art: A steel spoon and a plastic spoon, both with minus marks at the tip, and the steel spoon's marks flowing into a hand while the plastic spoon's stay put.

explanations.concept: Earthing: the Earth as a giant store
explanations.definition: Joining a charged thing to the ground with a conductor lets its extra charge flow into the Earth, which is so big that it hardly changes.
explanations.description: The Earth is a conductor, and it is enormous. If you give it a few billion extra electrons, or take a few billion away, nothing about it changes that anyone can measure. So it works like a bottomless drain or a bottomless store. When you touch a charged metal thing while standing on the floor, any extra charge can run through you to the Earth. This is why petrol tankers are joined to the ground when they load or unload fuel, and many trail a metal chain or strap, and why a three-pin plug has an earth pin. It is also why touching an earthed metal pipe calms the static on a paper sheet.
examples: A petrol tanker trails an earthing strap so charge cannot build up.
A three-pin plug has a long earth pin joined to the building's earth.
A person touching a metal almirah on a dry day may feel a small spark as charge drains away.
explanations.art: A petrol tanker with a metal chain trailing to the road, and below the road a drawing of the large Earth with small dots flowing into it.

explanations.concept: The push gets weaker quickly with distance
explanations.definition: The push or pull between two charges gets bigger with more charge and much smaller with more distance. Twice as far apart means only a quarter of the force.
explanations.description: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured this in France in 1785, with a very sensitive hanging balance. Two charges twice as far apart push a quarter as hard. Three times as far apart, a ninth as hard. Scientists call this an inverse square law. Sunlight also follows it: twice as far from a torch means the same light spread over four times the area. Gravity follows it too. The reason is geometry: whatever spreads out from a point in all directions thins out over the surface of a bigger and bigger sphere. This is why two balloons push hard when close and hardly at all when far apart. A bit of paper is pulled even more weakly from far away, because the balloon must first shift the paper's own charges. It is also why the charge on a single balloon can lift your hair but not move the table.
examples: Two charged balloons that push with some force at 1 centimetre push with a quarter of that force at 2 centimetres.
Two balloons with twice the charge each push four times as hard at the same distance.
A torch's light on a wall is a quarter as bright twice as far away.
explanations.art: Three dots in a row at distances 1, 2 and 3 with arrows of decreasing size, and beside them a grid showing light spreading from a torch over 1, 4 and 9 squares.

explanations.concept: A sharp point lets charge escape
explanations.definition: Charge crowds at sharp points of a conductor. The electric field there is strong enough to tear electrons from air, so charge leaks away into the air.
explanations.description: On a round metal ball, charge spreads out evenly. On a pointed piece of metal, charge crowds towards the tip, and the push on the air there is very strong. The air near the tip breaks down a little and carries the charge off in a faint, silent stream. Benjamin Franklin noticed this in the 1740s, and it is the reason a lightning conductor has a pointed top. It is also why the tinsel bars in printing presses are made of thin metal threads: each thread is a very fine point that lets charge leak away from passing paper. Scientists call this a corona discharge. Aircraft use the same trick: small wire wicks on the wings let charge leak off into the air.
examples: A lightning conductor on a building has a pointed tip.
A printing press uses a bar of fine metal threads to remove charge from paper.
A pin held near a charged balloon makes the balloon lose its charge quickly.
explanations.art: A pointed metal rod with a cloud of faint small dots leaving its tip into the air, next to a round metal ball with only a few dots.

explanations.definition: A spark happens when the push on the air between two charged things is so strong that the air suddenly lets charge through. Lightning is the same, on a giant scale.
explanations.description: Air is an insulator, until the push on it is strong enough. That takes about three million volts across each metre of air, or about 3,000 volts for each millimetre. A spark you can just feel from a door handle is across about one millimetre, so it takes about 3,000 volts. It hurts little because the amount of charge is very small and it passes in a flash. Lightning has hundreds of millions of volts and a huge amount of charge, so it is deadly. A bolt starts as a faint feeler that steps down from the cloud. When it is close to the ground, a bright return stroke travels up the same path from the ground to the cloud. The flash we see is the return stroke. The heated air bursts outward, which we hear as thunder.
examples: A static shock from a car door is a small spark.
A lightning flash is a spark many kilometres long.
Thunder is the sound of air heated to about 30,000 degrees Celsius bursting outward.
explanations.art: A storm cloud sending a faint branching feeler down to the ground, and a bright line rising back up the same path to the cloud.

explanations.concept: Static at work and static as a danger
explanations.definition: Static charge is used to put powder or paint exactly where we want it, and it is dangerous where sparks can set fire to fuel vapour or fine dust.
explanations.description: A laser printer charges a drum with a pattern, and the charged toner powder sticks only to the pattern. A paint spray gives each droplet the same charge, so droplets push apart into a fine mist and are pulled to the object being painted. A power station chimney can pass its smoke through charged plates so that the dust sticks to the plates instead of going into the sky. The same push is a problem in a flour mill or a fireworks factory, where one spark can ignite fine dust. At a petrol pump, fuel flowing through a hose builds up charge, and a spark could set fire to the vapour. So these places keep the air damp, wear cotton, and earth every metal part.
examples: A printer's toner sticks only where the drum is charged.
A power station's chimney plates catch dust from smoke.
A fuel tanker, a flour mill and a firework factory all earth their metal parts.
explanations.art: A laser printer drum with a pattern of charge and black powder sticking to it, next to a power station chimney with plates catching dust.

explanations.description: The air near the ground has a faint electric field, about 100 volts for every metre of height. In 2013 Dominic Clarke and colleagues showed that bumblebees can sense the weak electric field around a flower, and learn to tell flowers apart by it. A flying bee collects a small plus charge from the air, and a flower is usually minus, so pollen may jump to her without her touching it. In 2018 Erica Morley and Daniel Robert showed that spiders lift off on silk threads in an electric field, so charge helps them fly. Some fish, sharks and the platypus sense the fields made by other animals. Humans have no sense for it. Scientists do not yet know how common this is, or how many animals use it.
examples: A bumblebee senses the electric field of a flower before landing.
A spider lifts on a silk thread in an electric field.
A shark finds a hidden fish by the faint field the fish's muscles make.
explanations.art: A bumblebee flying towards a flower, with faint curved lines between them, and a spider on a leaf tip releasing a silk thread that rises in the air.

perspectives.explanation: Many animals live in a world full of electric fields and use them to find food and to move. People simply cannot sense them, so we had to build instruments to find out.
Some of the animal studies are small, and an animal reacting to a field does not prove she feels it as we feel touch. More careful tests are still being done.

agreed.text: Rubbing, or touching and pulling apart, moves electrons from one material to another, and the protons stay in the middle of the atoms.
agreed.evidence: A charge on a rubbed thing always has an equal and opposite charge on the thing it was rubbed with, as Faraday's pail experiment of 1843 and every later measurement show.

agreed.text: Charge is never made or destroyed. It is only moved from one place to another.
agreed.evidence: No experiment has ever found charge appearing from nothing or vanishing, and measurements of charge have been made to extreme accuracy.

agreed.text: There are two kinds of charge. The same kinds repel, and different kinds attract.
agreed.evidence: Du Fay's gold-leaf tests of 1733 and every test since: a rubbed glass tube and a rubbed resin rod act in opposite ways on the same leaf.

agreed.text: The force between two charges gets four times smaller each time the distance doubles.
agreed.evidence: Coulomb's balance measurements of 1785, and modern tests of this law that have found no difference from it.

agreed.text: Charge moves freely through metals and through salty water, and hardly at all through dry plastic, glass or rubber.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of how easily a charge flows through many materials, which sort them into conductors and insulators.

agreed.text: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity from charge that has separated in a storm cloud.
agreed.evidence: In 1752 sparks were drawn from an iron rod during a storm, and modern cameras and radio detectors record the current in every flash.

challenging.who: Many students and some old textbooks
challenging.for: Rubbing makes more charge than gentle touching, and rubbing warms things.
challenging.against: Clear tape pulled off a table is charged, and nobody rubbed it. Touching and separating is enough. Rubbing only helps by putting more of the two surfaces in contact. The charge is moved, not made by heat.

challenging.claim: Static electricity and the electricity in wires are two different kinds.
challenging.for: A rubbed rod made sparks, and a battery made a steady push. They looked and behaved very differently.
challenging.against: In 1833 Michael Faraday compared electricity from rubbing, from batteries, from magnets, from heat and from electric fish. He found they all did the same things. It is the same charge, behaving differently because of how it is arranged and moving.

challenging.claim: Two pieces of the same material cannot charge each other.
challenging.for: A ladder puts the same material at the same rung, so neither should win.
challenging.against: In 2011 Baytekin and colleagues, and in 2014 Waitukaitis and colleagues, found that identical materials can charge each other, because their surfaces are patchy or because of their size. Our simple ladder does not explain it.

challenging.claim: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
challenging.for: Most places are hit rarely, and a strike can seem like a once-only event.
challenging.against: Tall pointed things are hit again and again. The Empire State Building in New York is struck about 20 to 25 times a year.

challenging.claim: Electric charge is a fluid that is poured from one thing to another.
challenging.who: Benjamin Franklin and many of his time
challenging.for: It explained that charge can flow, that it is not made or lost, and it let Franklin make good predictions.
challenging.against: Charge is carried by particles, electrons mostly, which cannot be divided into tiny drops of fluid. The fluid picture was useful, but it led to a wrong guess about which way charge moves when glass is rubbed.

big_questions.q: Cotton takes electrons from wool and gives them to polythene. Is cotton a plus material or a minus material?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changed between the two rubs, and what did not.

big_questions.q: Charge cannot be made or destroyed. Where was the minus charge on your balloon before you rubbed it?
big_questions.hint: Think about the wool or hair, and about what a neutral thing really holds.

big_questions.q: A charged balloon pulls a plain wall. How does a wall with no extra charge feel the balloon, and how fast does it find out when the balloon moves?
big_questions.hint: Think about polarisation and the electric field around the balloon.

big_questions.q: Plus and minus were chosen by a guess, and the guess turned out backwards. If a name is wrong but works, should we change it?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a name is for, and what it would cost to change every book and every wire.

big_questions.q: A bee can feel a flower's electric field and you cannot. Does that mean you and the bee live in different worlds?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a sense does, and what you can know that a bee cannot.

big_questions.q: Around 2,800 people in India die each year from lightning, according to national crime records. Many are farmers working in open fields. Whose job is it to warn them, and how could the science help?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gets warnings in time, and which of them can see a storm coming.

big_questions.q: Static is a nuisance in a printing press and a tool in a laser printer. Is static good or bad?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether a thing can be harmful by itself, or only in a place.

big_questions.q: People have known about rubbed amber since ancient times, and scientists still argue about why it works. Why might a simple everyday thing stay a mystery?
big_questions.hint: Think about how hard it is to see what happens on a surface a few atoms thick.

story.title: The Sheets That Would Not Lie Flat
story.note: A made-up story set in a real town. Sivakasi is famous for printing and fireworks. The science is real: paper pulled over rollers picks up charge, and presses use an earthed bar of fine metal threads to take it away. The people and the press are imagined.
text: In Sivakasi, in the weeks before Deepavali, the printing presses never slept. Thenmozhi was ten. Every afternoon she carried her mother's lunch to the Lakshmi Offset Press in a steel tiffin carrier, and sat on a stool by the wall while her mother worked.

Her mother was Karpagam, and she ran the big printing machine. It took in a thin sheet of paper at one end. It printed red, green and gold on it, with a roar and a clatter. Then it slid the sheet out into a tray at the other end, and the sheet was a label for a box of crackers. A thousand sheets an hour should have made a neat, flat pile.

But that August the sheets would not lie flat. They slid out of the machine and rose at their edges like petals. They leaned away from each other. Some slid sideways off the pile, and some stuck to the iron frame of the tray. Karpagam had to straighten the pile by hand every few minutes, and the machine had to slow down. The orders were getting late.

Mr. Raghunathan, the owner, walked up and down with his hands behind his back. "It is the paper," he said. "The new supplier has sent us bad paper." So he brought out the old paper from the store. It did exactly the same.
"Then it is the machine," he said. He called Murugan, the mechanic, who opened the machine and looked for three hours. He found nothing wrong.

Thenmozhi ate her lunch and watched. She noticed a few things that nobody else was looking at. The sheets on top of the pile stood up the most. They leaned away from each other, like people who have just quarrelled. When she held out her arm, a loose sheet floated up and clung to her nylon sleeve, and the fine hairs on her arm stood up.
"Amma," she said, "the sheets do not like each other. They push."
"Paper does not push," said her mother, not unkindly. "Finish your lunch."

But Thenmozhi remembered something from school. Her science teacher, Mrs. Selvarani, had hung two balloons from one thread. She had rubbed both on her hair, and they swung apart. "Only things with the same kind of charge push each other away," Mrs. Selvarani had said.

So if the sheets were pushing, they all had the same kind of charge. But where did they get it? Thenmozhi looked at the rollers. Every sheet was pulled over the same rollers, a thousand times an hour. That was rubbing, wasn't it? And every sheet was rubbed in exactly the same way.

She had an idea for a test. The day was hot and dry. She picked up her steel tiffin carrier by its handle, and gently touched its lid to the top of the pile. The sheets under the lid sank flat, as if they had breathed out.
She touched the other corner. The sheets sank flat again. Then she tried the wooden handle of a broom in the same way. The sheets did not move at all.
"Mr. Raghunathan," she said, "please come and see."
He came, with his hands behind his back and one eyebrow raised. She showed him the steel and the wood, twice each. Steel made the sheets sink, and wood did nothing.
"The paper is not bad," she said. "It is full of charge from the rollers. The steel lets the charge run out of the paper, through my hand and my body, down into the floor. Wood will not let it go."
"Charge," said Mr. Raghunathan slowly. "Paper is paper." But then he stopped. "Last Thursday it rained all day," he said. "And the paper lay perfectly flat. I thought we had been lucky."
"Damp air lets charge leak away by itself," said Thenmozhi. "On a dry day it has nowhere to go."

Everyone in Sivakasi respects a spark. Mr. Raghunathan's cousin ran a cracker unit two lanes away, and he had never allowed anything near it that could jump a spark. He looked at the pile of sheets for a long time.
"Where does the charge go?" he said. "The machine stands on rubber pads, to stop the shaking. It cannot go into the floor from the machine."
"Then we must give it a path," said Thenmozhi. "A metal one, that goes to the ground."

Karpagam went to the cupboard in the corner, where she kept her good saree. She took out an old one with a silver zari border that was too worn to wear. She unpicked a long length of the shiny thread, which is made of fine metal. She wound one end round the iron pillar, which went down into the concrete floor. Then she spread the thread out at the other end, into a brush of a hundred fine strands, so that the paper slid right under them as it came out.
The machine started. The first sheet slid out under the silver strands and landed flat. So did the second. So did the hundredth. The pile grew straight and neat, as it should have.
"A hundred fine points," said Murugan, scratching his head. "The charge jumps off the paper into the air at each tip, and then goes down the thread and the pillar."
Mr. Raghunathan did not say anything for a while. Then he ordered a proper bar of fine steel bristles from Chennai, and until it came, the silver zari stayed where it was.

That Deepavali, labels printed on those sheets went onto cracker boxes in shops from Madurai to Mumbai. Nobody who bought them knew that the paper had once refused to lie flat, or that a girl on a stool had worked out why.
story.epiphany: For the parent: paper pulled over rollers touches and separates from them again and again, so it picks up a charge. Every sheet meets the same roller in the same way, so every sheet gets the same kind of charge. Sheets with the same charge push each other apart, which is why the pile fanned out. Neutral things such as a sleeve or the iron frame are pulled by the charged sheets. A steel carrier in her hand worked as a conductor, and the charge ran through her body to the floor. Wood is an insulator and did nothing. Damp air carries charge away by itself. The machine stood on rubber, so the charge had no path. Fine metal threads leak charge into the air at each tip, and an earth wire carries it down, which is what real press static eliminators do. Thenmozhi also did a fair test: she tried steel and wood twice each.
ask: Why would every sheet from the same rollers get the same kind of charge, and what does that do to a pile of sheets?
The steel carrier made the sheets sink flat, but a wooden broom handle did nothing. What does that tell you about steel and wood?
The same paper lay flat after a day of rain. Why might damp air stop a pile from fanning out?
A hundred fine threads took the charge away faster than one thick wire might. Why might a point be better than a flat plate at letting charge go?

roots.context: We have built a ladder of who gives electrons and who takes them, and followed charge into the ground. Now we ask what the ladder tells us about what a thing is.

deep_truth.truth: Cotton took electrons from wool and gave them to polythene. So cotton is neither a plus material nor a minus material. Plus and minus only describe how two things meet. Alone, a thing has no sign.
deep_truth.habit: We call a material positive or negative, as if the label belonged to the thing by itself. The ladder shows that the same cotton is minus against wool and plus against polythene, so the label belongs to the pair.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Charge Ladder, each material was rubbed on both wool and polythene, and the pushes on the balloon showed which way the electrons went. A material in the middle of the finished ladder takes from the rung above it and gives to the rung below it.

three.who_am_i: Your body is a conductor, so charge does not stay on you for long. It runs through you into the floor, and you are a path as well as a person.
three.what_is_life: A flying bee collects a small plus charge from the air, and a flower joined to the ground holds the opposite kind. Pollen can leap between them, so living things are part of the ladder too.
three.what_is_this_world: A spark, a tanker's chain and a lightning bolt all end in the same place, the Earth, which is large enough to take charge from anything.

roots.thread: One piece of cotton has no sign of its own. Put it next to wool, and it takes electrons. Put it next to polythene, and it gives them away. Charge never appeared from nowhere in any of your tests. It only moved, and the ground is the biggest place it can go. A clinging sheet, a spark and a lightning bolt are all the same thing, charge moving between things that happen to meet.

teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna argued that nothing has a nature of its own that stays the same whatever it meets. Things appear only in dependence on other things.
teachings.link: The same cotton gave electrons to one partner and took them from another. Its sign was not in the cotton alone. It was in the meeting.

teachings.teaching: Being and non-being give birth to each other. Hard and easy complete each other. Long and short shape each other, and high and low rest on each other.
teachings.link: A rung on the ladder is high only when something lower is there to give to, and low only when something higher is there to take from.

science.text: Only the two ends of the charge ladder always give or always take. A material in the middle gives to the rungs below it and takes from the rungs above it. Published ladders agree about the ends and disagree about close neighbours.
Why touching two materials moves charge between them is not yet agreed. Electrons, ions and tiny pieces of material have each been seen moving, and the same material can even charge itself.

other_view.view: Each material does have its own nature. It holds its outer electrons with a certain strength, and that can be measured. The ladder simply shows those strengths in order. A sign changes with the partner, but the strength belongs to the thing.

practice.title: Giver and taker
practice.say: Sit comfortably and close your eyes. Breathe in slowly and think that this air was made by plants. Breathe out slowly and think that this air goes to plants. Do this five times. Are you a giver or a taker?
practice.kid: Sit still. Breathe in slowly. This air came from plants. Breathe out. This air goes to plants. Do it five times. Are you a giver or a taker?

ask: The same cotton is plus with one partner and minus with another. Is anything plus or minus all on its own?
Charge is never made or destroyed. Where did the balloon's extra electrons come from, and where would they go if you touched it with a wet finger?
A bee and a flower hold opposite charges, and pollen jumps across. Which of them is the giver and which is the taker?
roots.art: A child standing on the middle rung of a tall ladder, one hand reaching up to receive small glowing dots from a person on the rung above and the other hand passing dots down to a person on the rung below.

games.title: Ladder Duel: who takes the electrons?
games.context: This is a card game about the charge ladder. You guess which of two materials takes the electrons, and which one gets the minus charge.

setup.art: Twelve material cards in a shuffled face-down pile beside a drawn board of twelve numbered rungs, with wool at rung 2 and PVC at rung 12.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the ladder board. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: The reader turning two cards face up, and the other players writing a guess on small slips of paper.
setup.caption: 2. Turn up two cards. Everyone guesses which gets the minus charge.

setup.caption: 3. Turn over the backs. The card with the bigger rung number gets the minus.

items.b: Rung 11 of 12. Near the bottom. It takes electrons from nearly everything above it.
