rules: Shuffle the 12 cards and put them face down in a pile. Lay the ladder board where everyone can see it.
The reader turns up two cards, with the material sides showing. The backs stay hidden. Neighbours are unreliable, so if the two cards are less than 3 rungs apart, put one back and draw another.
Every other player writes or says which of the two materials will get the minus charge when they are rubbed together. The reader then turns the cards over.
The card with the bigger rung number is lower on the ladder. It takes the electrons, so it gets the minus. A player with the right answer scores one point.
A player who also says why, using the words give, take or electrons, scores one more point.

For rounds 2 and 3, put all 12 cards back and shuffle again. In round 2, the reader turns up three cards, each at least 3 rungs from the others. Players name the one that is minus against both others, the one that is plus against both others, and the one in the middle. Getting all three right scores 2 points.

In round 3, the reader picks a card in the middle of the ladder, from rung 4 to rung 9. Players say its sign against the card three rungs above it and the card three rungs below it. A correct answer scores 2 points.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left. With two players, swap after every card.
Playing alone, draw two cards each turn and write your guess before you check. Score yourself in the same way. You win with 10 points from 12 cards.
The game ends when each player has been reader twice, or the pile is gone. The player with the most points wins. A tie is shared.

flow.do: Cut out the 12 cards and the ladder board. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. Give each player paper and a pencil for guesses.
flow.say: These cards are twelve materials on a charge ladder. In each round, you guess which one takes the electrons. Let us look at the board first.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the ladder. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ladder Duel. You set up the board and the cards.

flow.do: Play round 1. The reader turns up two cards at least 3 rungs apart. Everyone guesses which will get the minus charge. Turn over the backs and score. Play six pairs.
flow.say: Two cards are up. Which one will take the electrons and get the minus charge? Write your guess, then we turn the cards over.
flow.kid: Two cards are up. Which gets the minus? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why does the lower card get the minus charge?
good: Because it takes electrons from the higher card.
Because it is lower on the ladder.

flow.parent: Ask for the reason every time. The rule is always the same: the lower card takes electrons and gets the minus.
flow.context: In this step, you play round 1, with two cards at a time.

flow.do: Play round 2 with three cards at a time, and then round 3 with a middle card. Score the points as in the rules.
flow.say: Three cards are up. Which is minus against both the others? Which is plus against both? Which is in the middle?
flow.kid: Three cards are up. Which is minus, which is plus, which is in the middle?

ask.q: Why can the middle card be plus with one card and minus with another?
good: It gives to the ones below it and takes from the ones above.
Its partner changes.

flow.parent: The card in the middle is both. This is the main idea of the ladder: plus and minus belong to the meeting, not to the material.

check.q: A card is in the middle of the ladder. It meets one card above it and one below it. What happens?
options: It is minus with the one above and plus with the one below
It is plus with both
It is minus with both
check.why: A material takes electrons from those higher up, so it is minus with them. It gives electrons to those lower down, so it is plus with them. A card in the middle plays both roles.

flow.context: In this step, you play rounds 2 and 3, with a middle card that is both plus and minus.

flow.do: Count the points. Compare this ladder with the one from your own experiment. Where do the two ladders disagree? Talk about why.
flow.say: Count the points. Now compare this ladder with the one you built yourself. Do they match? Where do they differ, and why might that be?
flow.kid: Count your points. Compare this ladder with your own ladder.
flow.think: If two published ladders disagree about close neighbours, which should you trust?
flow.parent: Your ladder from the experiment may differ from this one. That is a normal result. Ladders agree about the ends, and not about close neighbours. Real data from your own home is worth more than a table in a book.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ladder Duel. You compare the game's ladder with your own.

experiments.title: The Charge Ladder: who gives electrons, and who takes them?
experiments.question: When five different things are each rubbed on wool and on polythene, which of them take electrons and which give them? Can the results be put in a ladder that predicts a pair you have not tried?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess for each of the five things. After wool, will it push the balloon away? After polythene, will it push or pull? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Every thing gets ten strokes, always in one direction. Every thing is held 3 centimetres from the balloon, at the same height, for 5 seconds. Each thing is wiped clean before the next test, and the hanging balloon is charged again on wool after every three tests. The same wool, the same polythene and the same room are used all the way through. Only the thing being rubbed changes.

materials.item: a balloon, blown up to about 25 centimetres across, with 40 centimetres of thread tied to it
a pencil and cello tape, to hang the balloon from the edge of a table
a dry woollen shawl, muffler or sweater, folded flat
a clean, dry plastic carry bag, cut open and laid flat, about 30 centimetres square

the five things to test: a hard plastic ruler, a plastic comb, a second blown-up balloon, a tube of paper rolled from one A4 sheet and taped, and a wad of cotton cloth held on the neck of an empty plastic bottle with a rubber band
a damp cloth and a dry cloth, for wiping the charge off between tests
7 small paper cards and the results table

experiments.safety: Balloons and small cut pieces can choke young children, so keep them away from children under three. If anyone at home has a latex allergy, do not use latex balloons. Do this indoors, in a room away from the kitchen gas, and never during a thunderstorm.
experiments.record: Fill in the results table for all five things. Then lay the seven cards in a ladder with wool at the top and polythene at the bottom, and draw it.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you rub five things on wool and on polythene, and use a hanging balloon to see which way the charge went. Then you build a ladder from your results.

setup.art: A balloon hanging by a 40-centimetre thread from a pencil taped to a table edge, with a child rubbing it along a folded woollen shawl.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the balloon from the table edge. Charge it on the wool.

setup.art: A plastic ruler being rubbed ten times along a folded woollen shawl lying flat on a table.
setup.caption: 2. Rub the first thing ten times along the wool, always one way.

setup.art: The rubbed ruler held 3 centimetres from the hanging balloon, which swings away from it, with an arrow and the letter R.
setup.caption: 3. Hold it near the balloon. R means the balloon is pushed away.

setup.art: The same ruler being rubbed along a flat plastic bag on the table, and then held near the balloon, which swings towards it, with the letter A.
setup.caption: 4. Wipe the thing clean. Rub it along the polythene. A means the balloon is pulled closer.

setup.art: Seven small cards laid in a column as a ladder, with the word wool on the top card and the word polythene on the bottom card, and five cards in between.
setup.caption: 5. Put the cards in a ladder from your results.

flow.do: Lay out the five things, the wool and the polythene. Ask your child to guess for each thing, and to say why. Write every guess down.
flow.say: We will rub five things on wool, and then on polythene. Which will take electrons and push our balloon away? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which things will push the balloon away. Say why.

ask.q: Which thing do you think will charge the most, and why?
good: The balloon, because it worked before.
The plastic ruler, because plastic holds charge.
I am not sure, but the cloth looks too soft.

flow.parent: Write the guesses and reasons at the top of the table. Do not correct them. Some will be right by luck, and that is fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Charge Ladder. You guess before you test, and you say why.

flow.do: Blow up the first balloon and tie 40 centimetres of thread to it. Tie the other end to a pencil. Tape the pencil to the edge of a table so the balloon hangs free, 30 centimetres from any wall. Rub the hanging balloon ten times along the wool, in one direction. Step back until it stops swinging. Hold your plain hand 5 centimetres away and watch the balloon.
flow.say: This hanging balloon is our detector. We charge it on wool. Now hold your plain hand near it. What does it do?
flow.kid: Hang a balloon from the table edge. Rub it ten times on wool. Hold your hand near.

ask.q: The balloon leaned towards your plain hand. Does that mean your hand is charged?
good: No. A pull does not prove it.
A plain hand has no extra charge, but it still pulled.

flow.parent: The balloon should lean gently towards your hand. If it does not, rub it ten more times. On a damp day, use an air-conditioned room. Or a grown-up can blow a hair dryer on the cool setting, held 30 centimetres away, on the wool for 30 seconds first. Never aim it at the balloon, because heat can burst it. Charge fades in about a minute, so you will recharge it often.

check.q: The charged balloon leans towards your plain hand. What does that show?
options: Your hand has a charge
A pull alone does not prove the other thing is charged
The balloon has lost its charge
check.why: A charged balloon pulls on neutral things too, because it shifts their own charges a little. So a pull is not proof. Only a push shows that both things have the same kind of charge. Pick the first option, and you will think every pull means a charge.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the balloon, charge it and see that a plain hand pulls it. This balloon is the detector for the rest of the test.

flow.do: Hold the plain, unrubbed ruler 3 centimetres from the balloon, at the same height. Watch for 5 seconds. Write R if the balloon is pushed away, A if it is pulled closer, and 0 if nothing happens.
flow.say: First, a control. This ruler has not been rubbed. What does the balloon do? Write R, A or 0.
flow.kid: Hold the plain ruler near the balloon. Write R, A or 0.

ask.q: Why do we test a ruler we have not rubbed?
good: To see what a plain ruler does.
To have something to compare with.
To check the ruler is not already charged.

flow.parent: Often the balloon leans a little towards the plain ruler. That is polarisation, and it is why we trust only a push. If the balloon moves away from a plain ruler, the ruler already has a charge. Wipe it with a damp cloth, dry it, and try again.
flow.context: In this step, you test a ruler that has not been rubbed. This is the control that you compare the other tests with.

flow.do: Lay the folded wool flat on the table. Rub the first thing along the wool, ten strokes, always one way. Carry it to the balloon and hold it 3 centimetres away. Watch for 5 seconds and write R, A or 0. Wipe the thing with a damp hand, then dry it. Do all five things. Recharge the balloon on the wool after every three tests.
flow.say: Ten strokes, one way, then carry it over. Does the balloon move away, move closer, or stay still? Write R, A or 0.
flow.kid: Rub a thing ten times on wool. Hold it near the balloon. Write R, A or 0.

ask.q: What does an R tell you about the thing you rubbed?
good: It has the same kind of charge as the balloon.
It took electrons from the wool.
Both are minus.

flow.parent: Expect the ruler, the comb and the balloon to push the hanging balloon away. The paper tube and the cotton often give a weak push or nothing. If nothing moves at all, give twenty strokes, move the thing in slowly from the side, or try again in a drier room. Write 0. A weak charge is a real result.

check.q: A ruler rubbed on wool pushes the balloon away. What do you know about the ruler?
options: It has the same kind of charge as the balloon
It has no charge
It has the opposite kind of charge
check.why: A push needs the same kind of charge on both things. The balloon took electrons from the wool, so it is minus. So the ruler is minus too, and it took electrons from the wool. If you picked no charge, remember that no charge gives a pull at most.

flow.context: In this step, you rub each of the five things on wool and test it against the balloon. You write R, A or 0 for each.

flow.do: Lay the polythene flat on the table. Rub the first thing along the polythene, ten strokes, always one way. Carry it to the balloon and hold it 3 centimetres away. Watch for 5 seconds and write R, A or 0. Wipe the thing clean. Do all five things. Recharge the balloon on the wool after every three tests.
flow.say: Now the same five things on polythene. Does each one push the balloon away, pull it closer, or do nothing? Write R, A or 0.
flow.kid: Now rub each thing on polythene. Hold it near the balloon. Write R, A or 0.

ask.q: A thing pulls the balloon after polythene, and pushed it after wool. What could that mean?
good: It took electrons from wool and gave some to polythene.
It is between them.
It has the opposite charge with polythene.

flow.parent: Expect different results from step 4. The paper tube and the cotton often pull the balloon after polythene, because they gave electrons to the polythene. Remember that a pull is only a hint. Do not worry if some results are messy. Write down what you saw.
flow.context: In this step, you rub the same five things on polythene and test them again. Some may behave differently from before.

flow.do: Cut seven small cards: wool, polythene, and the five things. Put wool at the top and polythene at the bottom. A thing that pushed the balloon after wool goes below wool. A thing that pushed it after wool and pulled it after polythene goes in the middle. Now pick two things that are far apart on your ladder. Say which will get the minus charge. Rub them together, test each one on the balloon, and check.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Put the cards in a ladder. Pick two far apart. Rub them together. Test your guess.
flow.think: Which of your five things sits in the middle of the ladder, and what does that mean?

ask.q: Which thing gives electrons to some partners and takes them from others?
good: The one in the middle.
Cotton, or paper.
The thing that pushed after wool but pulled after polythene.

flow.parent: Only after they have said what they saw, explain: each thing can give to the ones lower on the ladder and take from the ones higher. So a thing in the middle is plus with one partner and minus with another. Your ladder may not match a book's. Books disagree about close neighbours, and damp air changes the order.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Charge Ladder. You build your ladder and use it to predict a pair you have not tried.

experiments.title: Two Balloons: does twice the rubbing push twice as far?
experiments.question: Two balloons rubbed the same number of times hang apart in a V. Does ten rubs make the gap twice as big as five rubs? Does twenty rubs make it four times as big?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess how far apart the balloons will hang after 5, 10 and 20 rubs. Will 20 rubs give a gap four times as big as 5? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Both balloons are the same size, hang on threads of the same length from the same pencil, and are rubbed on the same wool with the same number of strokes. The gap is measured 10 seconds after hanging, between the same two knots. The balloons are cleared of charge between levels. Only the number of rubs changes.

materials.item: 2 balloons blown up to the same size, about 20 centimetres across, each with 60 centimetres of thread ending in a loop
a pencil and cello tape, to hang them side by side from the edge of a table
a dry woollen shawl or sweater
a 30-centimetre ruler or a measuring tape
a damp cloth and a dry cloth
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Keep balloons and bits of burst balloon away from children under three. If anyone at home has a latex allergy, do not use latex balloons.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each number of rubs, using the gap beyond the resting gap.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you charge two balloons the same amount and measure how far apart they hang. You find out whether more rubbing pushes them proportionally further.

setup.art: Two blown-up balloons hanging side by side from loops over a pencil taped to a table edge, touching each other at rest, with a ruler held at the knots.
setup.caption: 1. Hang both balloons from one pencil. Measure the gap between the knots at rest.

setup.art: A child rubbing one balloon along a woollen shawl, counting strokes aloud, with the other balloon waiting beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Rub each balloon the same number of times on the wool.

setup.art: The two balloons hanging apart in a V shape with a ruler measuring the gap between their knots.
setup.caption: 3. Hang them again. Wait 10 seconds. Measure the gap between the knots.

flow.do: Show your child the two balloons, the wool and the ruler. Ask for a guess about the gap after 5, 10 and 20 rubs, and for a reason. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will rub two balloons the same amount and see how far apart they hang. Will 20 rubs push them four times as far as 5 rubs? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how far apart the balloons will hang. Say why.

ask.q: Do you think the gap will double when the rubs double? Why?
good: Yes, because twice the charge pushes twice as hard.
No, because the balloons are heavy and pull back.
Not sure. Let us test.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Both a doubling guess and a not-doubling guess are good starting points.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Balloons test. You guess before you measure.

flow.do: Tie each thread to a loop. Slip both loops over the middle of the pencil. Tape the pencil to the edge of a table so the balloons hang free and touch each other. Measure the distance between the two knots. Write it down as the resting gap.
flow.say: Both balloons hang from one point and touch each other. Measure the gap between the knots. This is the resting gap, before any charge.
flow.kid: Hang both balloons from one pencil. Measure the gap between the knots.
flow.parent: The resting gap will be about 20 centimetres, the width of a balloon. Measure from knot to knot every time. Keep the balloons away from walls.
flow.context: In this step, you hang the two balloons and measure how far apart they are before any rubbing.

flow.do: Lift both loops off the pencil. Rub the first balloon 5 times on the wool, then the second balloon 5 times. Slip the loops back over the pencil. Wait 10 seconds. Measure the gap between the knots. Repeat once more. Then touch both balloons with a damp hand and wait 30 seconds.
flow.say: Five rubs for each balloon, always the same direction. Hang them up again. Wait ten seconds, and measure the gap. Write it down.
flow.kid: Rub each balloon 5 times. Hang them. Measure the gap.

ask.q: Why do the balloons hang apart now?
good: They both have the same kind of charge.
They both took electrons from the wool.
Two minus charges push each other away.

flow.parent: Measure at 10 seconds each time, because the charge leaks away. Do two tries. If the gap is nearly the same as the resting gap, rub six more times.
flow.context: In this step, you rub both balloons five times each and measure how far apart they hang.

flow.do: Repeat step 3 with 10 rubs on each balloon. Do two tries, and clear the charge with a damp hand afterwards.
flow.say: Now ten rubs each. Hang them up, wait ten seconds, and measure. Is the gap twice as big as with five rubs?
flow.kid: Rub each balloon 10 times. Hang them. Measure the gap.

ask.q: Is the gap twice as big as before? What does it tell you?
good: It is bigger but not twice as big.
More rubbing gives more charge, so more push.
Maybe some charge leaked away.

flow.parent: Do not tell your child the answer. The gap should grow, but usually by less than double.
flow.context: In this step, you rub each balloon ten times. You compare the new gap with the last one.

flow.do: Repeat step 3 with 20 rubs on each balloon. Do two tries, and clear the charge with a damp hand afterwards.
flow.say: Now twenty rubs each. Hang them up, wait ten seconds, and measure. How does this gap compare with the others?
flow.kid: Rub each balloon 20 times. Hang them. Measure the gap.

check.q: Two balloons rubbed 20 times each hang further apart than after 5 rubs. What does this show?
options: More rubbing gave each balloon more charge, so they push harder
The balloons became lighter
The wool pushed the balloons apart
check.why: Each rub moves more electrons onto the balloon, so each balloon has more charge, and the push between them is bigger. The balloons do not get lighter, and the wool is far away by then.

flow.context: In this step, you rub each balloon twenty times and measure the gap one last time.

flow.do: Subtract the resting gap from each gap. Draw a bar chart with one bar for 5, 10 and 20 rubs. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each number of rubs. Say what you saw.
flow.think: If you could rub forever, would the gap keep growing?
flow.parent: After they have said what they saw, explain: more rubs moved more electrons, so each balloon had more charge and pushed harder. But the gap did not grow in step, for two reasons. The push gets weaker as the balloons move apart. And the balloons can hold only so much charge before it leaks into the air as tiny sparks you cannot see.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Two Balloons test. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

activities.title: The Foil Ball That Changes Its Mind

materials.item: kitchen foil, 5 centimetres square
30 centimetres of sewing thread, a pencil and cello tape
a balloon, blown up and tied
a dry woollen shawl or sweater

schedule.what: Make the foil ball. Watch what it does near a charged balloon. Touch it with a finger.

activities.record: Draw the foil ball three times: before the balloon, just after it touches, and after you touch it with your finger. Add arrows for what happens.
activities.context: In this activity, you hang a little foil ball near a charged balloon and watch it change what it does. This is the thing to notice before the explanations.

setup.art: A small ball of foil on a thread hanging from a pencil taped to the edge of a table.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a foil ball from the table edge.

setup.art: A charged balloon held near the foil ball, and the ball swinging towards the balloon and touching it.
setup.caption: 2. Bring the balloon near. The ball jumps to it.

setup.art: The foil ball hanging away from the balloon, with the balloon following it and the ball swinging further away.
setup.caption: 3. A moment later, the ball is pushed away.

setup.art: A finger touching the foil ball, and then the ball swinging back towards the balloon.
setup.caption: 4. Touch the ball with your finger. It is pulled to the balloon again.

flow.do: Tear a piece of foil 5 centimetres square. Scrunch it around the end of the thread into a ball the size of a marble. Tie the other end to a pencil. Tape the pencil to the edge of a table so the ball hangs free.
flow.say: This foil ball hangs on a thread. Foil is a metal. Before we use it, what do you think will happen when a charged balloon comes near?
flow.kid: Make a foil ball on a thread. Hang it from a table edge.

ask.q: What do you think the ball will do when the charged balloon comes near, and why?
good: It will move towards the balloon, because it is light.
It will be pulled, like paper.
It will move away.

flow.parent: Keep the foil ball smooth, with no sharp points. Silk thread is best, and cotton works too. Write your child's guess down.
flow.context: In this step, you make a foil ball on a thread. You guess what it will do before you test.

flow.do: Rub a balloon 15 times on the wool. Hold it slowly towards the ball, from the side, until it is about 5 centimetres away. Let the ball touch the balloon. Watch what happens next.
flow.say: Fifteen rubs on wool. Now bring the balloon slowly to the ball. What does the ball do? What does it do after it touches?
flow.kid: Rub the balloon on wool. Bring it near the ball. Watch.

ask.q: What did the ball do first, and what did it do after it touched the balloon?
good: First it jumped to the balloon, then it was pushed away.
It was pulled, and then it was repelled.

flow.parent: The ball should jump to the balloon, touch it, and then swing away. If it does not, rub the balloon ten more times. Try a drier room if you can. Do not explain yet.

check.q: The foil ball touched the balloon, and then it was pushed away. What does that show?
options: The ball took some of the balloon's charge, so both now have the same kind of charge
The ball became heavier
The balloon lost all its charge
check.why: Touching let some electrons run from the balloon onto the metal ball. Now both have minus charge, and two minus charges push apart. The ball did not get heavier, and the balloon kept most of its charge.

flow.context: In this step, you bring a charged balloon to the foil ball. You watch it jump, touch and then swing away.

flow.do: Move the balloon slowly towards the ball again. Try to chase the ball with the balloon. Watch how it runs away.
flow.say: Chase the ball with the balloon. What does it do? Why do you think it runs away now, and it did not before?
flow.kid: Chase the ball with the balloon. What does it do?

ask.q: Why does the ball run away from the balloon now, when before it jumped to it?
good: Now it has the same charge as the balloon.
It took charge when it touched.

flow.parent: The ball should swing away as you push the balloon towards it. Wait for your child to say why, before you explain.
flow.context: In this step, you chase the ball with the balloon. You watch it keep away.

flow.do: Touch the ball with your finger for two seconds. Then bring the balloon near again. Watch what the ball does now. Draw it three times.
flow.say: Touch the ball with your finger. Now bring the balloon near. What does it do now? Where did the ball's charge go?
flow.kid: Touch the ball with your finger. Bring the balloon near. Draw it.

ask.q: Where did the ball's charge go when you touched it?
good: It ran through my finger and my body into the floor.
My body took it away.

flow.parent: The ball should jump to the balloon again. Your finger and body let the extra charge run away into the floor. Then say that the ball can do this over and over.
flow.context: In this step, you touch the ball with a finger and watch it change its mind once more.

activities.title: Charge Walk: which things let charge run away?

materials.item: the foil ball on a thread, hung from a table edge, and a balloon
a dry woollen shawl or sweater
a steel spoon, a plastic spoon, a wooden spoon, a pencil, a strip of dry paper, a coin and a cotton thread
a tray of water for a wet fingertip, and a towel
the results table and a pencil

schedule.what: Charge the foil ball. Touch it with each thing. Test with the balloon if the ball is still charged.

activities.record: A table with each thing, your guess, what the ball did, and two groups at the end: lets charge run away, and keeps the charge.
activities.context: In this activity, you charge a foil ball and then touch it with different things. The ball shows which things let the charge run away through your hand.

setup.art: A foil ball on a thread, pushed away from a charged balloon after touching it.
setup.caption: 1. Charge the foil ball by touching it with the balloon.

setup.art: A steel spoon held by its handle in a hand, with its tip touching the foil ball.
setup.caption: 2. Touch the ball with one thing, held in your hand.

setup.art: A fresh charged balloon brought near the foil ball, which is either pushed away or pulled towards it.
setup.caption: 3. Test the ball with a charged balloon. Pushed away means the charge is still there.

flow.do: Line up the seven things and a wet fingertip. Ask your child to guess, for each thing, if it will let the charge run away or keep it. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will charge the foil ball, then touch it with each of these. Which things let the charge run away, and which keep it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess for each thing. Does it let charge run away?

ask.q: Which one are you most sure about, and why?
good: The steel spoon, because metal carries things.
The plastic spoon, because plastic stops it.
My finger, because I am wet.

flow.parent: Write the guesses down. Do not correct them. Your body will be part of the test, because you are holding each thing.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Charge Walk. You guess for each thing.

flow.do: Rub a balloon 15 times on the wool. Touch it to the foil ball and let the ball swing away. Hold the steel spoon by its handle and touch the tip to the ball for two seconds. Then bring the charged balloon near the ball and watch.
flow.say: The ball is charged. Touch it with the steel spoon in your hand. Then bring the balloon near. Does the ball run away, or come to the balloon?
flow.kid: Charge the ball. Touch it with the steel spoon. Test with the balloon.

ask.q: The ball came to the balloon after the spoon. What did the spoon do?
good: It let the charge run away.
The charge went through the spoon and my body.

flow.parent: A ball that is pulled towards the balloon has lost its charge. A ball that is pushed away still has it. The steel spoon should leave the ball plain. Recharge the ball by touching it with the balloon before every new test.
flow.context: In this step, you charge the ball and test it with the steel spoon in your hand.

flow.do: Recharge the ball each time. Touch it for two seconds with each of the other things. For the pencil, touch the ball with the lead tip. Then test with the balloon, and write down if the ball still pushes away, or comes closer. Finally, try a dry fingertip and a wet fingertip.
flow.say: Recharge the ball. Touch it with the next thing. Then test it with the balloon. Is the charge still there, or has it run away?
flow.kid: Recharge the ball. Touch it with a thing. Test with the balloon.

check.q: A plastic spoon touches the charged ball. The ball is still pushed away by the balloon. What does this show?
options: Plastic does not let the charge run away
Plastic is a conductor
The ball has no charge
check.why: If the charge had run away, the ball would have been pulled closer. It was still pushed, so the charge stayed on the ball. That is what an insulator does. A conductor would have let it go, through your hand and body.

flow.parent: Expect the steel spoon, the coin, the pencil lead and your fingers to remove the charge. The plastic spoon and the dry paper keep it. The wooden spoon may remove a little, slowly. A damp day makes more things conduct.
flow.context: In this step, you test the other things in the same way.

flow.do: Sort the seven things into two groups: those that let the charge run away, and those that kept it. Ask your child what the first group has in common.
flow.say: Sort the things into two groups. What do the things in the first group have in common?
flow.kid: Sort the things into two groups. Say what the first group shares.
flow.think: Where did the charge go when it ran away?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the charge ran along metal or through the body into the floor. After they have said it, tell them that the Earth works as a giant store for charge.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the things into two groups.

activities.title: Tape Twins: one peel, two charges

materials.item: a roll of clear cello tape, about 2 centimetres wide
a smooth, clean, dry table top or a plastic tray
a pen and a small piece of paper for labels

schedule.what: Make two pairs of tape twins. Pull each pair apart. See which push and which pull.

activities.record: Draw the four strips and write T or B on each. Write which pairs pushed apart and which pulled together.
activities.context: In this activity, you peel two strips of tape apart and find that they carry opposite charges. You see both kinds of charge at once, without any cloth.

setup.art: A strip of clear tape stuck on a table with a second strip stuck on top of it, both with a folded end for a handle.
setup.caption: 1. Stick one strip on the table. Stick another strip on top of it.

setup.art: The two stuck strips being peeled off the table together by their handles, then pulled apart quickly.
setup.caption: 2. Peel both off together. Then pull them apart quickly.

setup.art: Two strips hanging from a table edge, with a third strip held between them, pushing one away and pulling the other closer.
setup.caption: 3. Hang the strips. See which push apart and which pull together.

flow.do: Tear four strips of tape, each 20 centimetres long. Fold over 1 centimetre at one end of each strip to make a handle. Stick two strips firmly on the table. Press the other two on top of them. Label the strips on the table B, and the ones on top T.
flow.say: We have two pairs of strips. The strips on the table are B for bottom. The strips on top are T. Before we peel them, what do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Stick two strips on the table. Press two more on top. Label them B and T.

ask.q: What do you think will happen when we peel a pair apart, and why?
good: They will stick to each other.
They might get charged, like the balloon.
Nothing will happen.

flow.parent: Press each strip down well with a finger, but leave the handles free. Keep the strips clean and dry. A bit of dust spoils the result, and a damp day weakens it.
flow.context: In this step, you make two pairs of tape strips stuck on top of each other.

flow.do: Hold the handles of the first pair. Peel both strips off the table together in one smooth pull. Then pull the two strips apart quickly. Hang each strip by its handle from the edge of the table. Do the second pair in the same way.
flow.say: Peel both strips off together. Then pull them apart fast. Hang them by their handles. What do you notice about how they hang?
flow.kid: Peel a pair off the table. Pull the strips apart fast. Hang them.

ask.q: What do you notice about how the strips hang?
good: They swing towards or away from things.
They are not straight.
They seem to cling to me.

flow.parent: Pull the strips apart in one quick movement, because slow pulling lets the charge leak. Strips should swing towards your hand. If they do not, try a drier room.
flow.context: In this step, you peel each pair apart and hang the strips.

flow.do: Bring the two T strips close to each other. Then bring the two B strips close to each other. Then bring a T strip close to a B strip. Write push or pull for each.
flow.say: Bring two T strips together. Do they push or pull? Now two B strips. Now a T and a B. Write down what you see.
flow.kid: Bring the strips close. Do they push or pull? Write it down.

ask.q: Which pairs of strips pushed apart, and which pulled together?
good: T and T pushed. B and B pushed. T and B pulled.
The same labels pushed, and different labels pulled.

flow.parent: Expect two Ts to push apart, two Bs to push apart, and a T and a B to pull together. This shows two kinds of charge from one peel. Do not say yet which is plus and which is minus. Nobody can tell from this test alone.

check.q: Two T strips push apart. A T strip and a B strip pull together. What does this show?
options: T and B carry opposite kinds of charge
T and B carry the same kind of charge
Only T is charged
check.why: Same kinds of charge push apart, and different kinds pull together. The two Ts push, so they have the same kind. A T and a B pull, so they have opposite kinds. If B were neutral it would pull a T only weakly, and the two Bs would not push each other.

flow.context: In this step, you test which strips push and which pull. This tells you if the charges are the same or opposite.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain what happened. Ask where the charges came from when nobody rubbed anything.
flow.say: Nobody rubbed these strips. Where did the charge come from? Why do the top and bottom strips have opposite charges?
flow.kid: Where did the charge come from? Say what you think.
flow.think: If the charges are equal and opposite, what would happen if you pressed the two strips together again?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that peeling moved electrons from one strip to the other, so one has extra and the other has a shortage. Pressing them together lets the electrons go back, and the strips become neutral again.
flow.context: In this step, you say where the charge came from.

projects.title: Our Home Ladder: does the order change on a damp day?

materials.item: the hanging balloon, the folded wool and the polythene from the Charge Ladder test
four new dry things from your home that are not metal, for example a plastic bangle, a nylon or silk cloth wad on a bottle, a thermocol plate and a rubber slipper
a damp cloth and a dry cloth
a notebook for three days of results

schedule.what: Choose four new things. Guess their rungs. Test each on wool and on polythene in a dry room.
Test the same four things in a damp place, for example a bathroom after a hot shower.
Compare the two days. Draw your final ladder with all nine rungs.

projects.record: A table with three columns: the thing, its result on the dry day, its result on the damp day. Then a final ladder with all nine rungs.
projects.context: In this project, you add four new things to your ladder, and then test them again in damp air to see whether the order changes.

setup.art: Four new things laid in a row beside a folded woollen shawl and a flat plastic bag: a plastic bangle, a cloth wad on a bottle, a thermocol plate and a rubber slipper.
setup.caption: 1. Choose four new things that are dry and not metal.

setup.art: A child testing a plastic bangle near a hanging balloon in a dry room, with a notebook open beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Day 1: test each thing on wool and polythene in a dry room.

setup.art: The same child testing the bangle in a damp bathroom with a grown-up beside her and no electric appliances nearby.
setup.caption: 3. Day 2: test them again in a damp place.

flow.do: Choose four new things that are dry and not metal. Lay them out and guess where each will sit on your ladder from the Charge Ladder test. Write the guesses and reasons in the notebook.
flow.say: We will add four new things to our ladder. Where will each one sit? Is it near wool, near polythene, or in the middle? Why?
flow.kid: Pick four new things. Guess where each goes on your ladder.
flow.parent: Do not worry about being right. Writing the guess first is what matters. If you have no thermocol, use a plastic bottle, a foam slipper or a nylon cloth.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Home Ladder project. You choose and guess before testing.

flow.do: Hang and charge the balloon as before. Rub each new thing ten times on the wool and then on the polythene. Hold each 3 centimetres from the balloon and write R, A or 0. Wipe each one clean before the next test.
flow.say: The same test as before, with four new things. Rub ten times, hold it near the balloon, and write R, A or 0.
flow.kid: Test each new thing on wool and polythene. Write R, A or 0.

check.q: A new thing pushes the balloon away after wool, and also after polythene. Where does it sit on the ladder?
options: Below both wool and polythene
Between wool and polythene
Above both wool and polythene
check.why: A push after wool means the thing took electrons from wool, so it is below wool. A push after polythene means it took electrons from polythene too, so it is below polythene. That puts it at the very bottom of your ladder.

flow.context: In this step, you test your four new things in a dry room.

flow.wait: Do this on another day, in a damp place such as a bathroom after a hot shower.
flow.do: On the second day, hang the balloon in a damp place. Test the same four things on wool and polythene in the same way. Write R, A or 0 for each, in a new column.
flow.say: Today the air is damp. Do the same tests as before. Do the things push the balloon as strongly? Why might that be?
flow.kid: Test the same things in damp air. Write R, A or 0.

ask.q: Did the damp air change your results? How?
good: The pushes were weaker.
Some things did nothing.
The balloon lost its charge quickly.

flow.parent: Expect weaker pushes, or none. The charge leaks away through the thin film of water on every surface. If you get no results at all, that is the result: write 0. A grown-up should stay in the room, because wet floors are slippery. Keep the tap water cool and keep every plug and electric appliance well away. Do not try to dry the things with a heater.
flow.context: In this step, you repeat the tests in damp air.

flow.wait: Do this on the third day.
flow.do: Put the two columns side by side. Did the order of the things change? Draw your final ladder with all nine rungs. Write three sentences about what you found.
flow.say: Look at both columns. Did the order change on the damp day? Or only how strongly they pushed? What do you think that tells us?
flow.kid: Compare the two days. Draw your ladder with nine rungs.
flow.think: If damp air weakens the pushes but keeps the order, what is the water doing?
flow.parent: Many families find that the order stays but the pushes weaken, because water on the surface lets charge leak. Some find the order shifts a little. Both are real results. Published ladders also disagree, partly for this reason.
flow.context: This is the last day of the Home Ladder project. You compare the two days and draw your final ladder.

challenges.title: Stop the Cling: make a charged strip fall off the wall
challenges.problem: A strip of polythene, 30 centimetres by 5 centimetres, is rubbed ten times on wool and pressed on a wall. It clings. Find a way to make it fall off within 5 seconds, using only things from your home, and without wetting the strip.
constraints: Cut the strip from a clean, dry plastic bag. Use the same size every time.
Rub it ten times on the wool, in one direction, before each try.
You may do one thing to the strip or near it, in the first 3 seconds after you press it on the wall.
You may not wet the strip or heat it. Do not use a flame.
Time each try with a timer, and do each idea three times.
materials: a clean, dry plastic carry bag and scissors
a dry woollen shawl or sweater
kitchen foil, a steel spoon, cotton thread and a pencil
a timer, a pen and paper
general: Touch the strip with a steel spoon held in your hand, so the charge can run through you to the floor.
Wipe the strip with your bare hand.
Hold a metal spoon or a foil strip near it without touching.
creative: Make a brush of thin foil strips taped to a pencil, and wave it over the strip so each fine tip leaks charge.
Press the strip onto the wall next to a steel almirah or a metal pipe, and see if the charge drains away.
Use a damp bathroom for the whole test and see whether the strip falls faster.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your idea first. Build it and test it three times. Write the times. Change one thing, and test again. Which idea made the strip fall fastest? Why do you think it worked?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about charge. You find ways to let the charge leave a strip, using what you know about conductors and points.

setup.art: A child pressing a polythene strip onto a wall after rubbing it on wool, with a timer beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Rub the strip ten times on wool. Press it on the wall and start the timer.

setup.art: A child touching a steel spoon held in her hand to the strip on the wall, and the strip starting to slide down.
setup.caption: 2. Try your idea in the first 3 seconds.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a table of ideas and the times for each of three tries.
setup.caption: 3. Write the three times for each idea.

flow.do: Cut one strip, 30 centimetres by 5 centimetres. Rub it ten times on the wool and press it on the wall. Time how long it stays up with nothing done to it. Do this three times.
flow.say: First, how long does the strip cling if we do nothing? Time it three times. This is the number we must beat.
flow.kid: Rub the strip. Press it on the wall. Time how long it stays up.

ask.q: Why do we time the strip when we do nothing to it?
good: To have a number to beat.
So we know what the idea changes.

flow.parent: On a dry day, the strip may stay up for a minute or more. On a damp day it may fall in seconds, and then you have already found one answer. Try again in a drier room.
flow.context: In this step, you time how long the charged strip clings to the wall.

flow.do: Sketch two or three ideas for making the charge leave the strip. Choose one to test first.
flow.say: How could we let the charge leave the strip? Think of what ran charge away in the Charge Walk. Draw two or three ideas.
flow.kid: Draw two ideas for making the strip fall. Pick one.

ask.q: Which things would let the charge run away, and why?
good: Metal, because it is a conductor.
My hand, because I am a conductor.
Something pointed, because charge leaks off points.

flow.parent: Remember what you learned about conductors and points. There is no single right answer. Any idea with a reason is a good one to test.
flow.context: In this step, you draw ideas for removing the charge.

flow.do: Test your first idea three times. Rub the strip ten times each time, and use your idea only in the first 3 seconds. Write the times in a table. Then test your second idea in the same way.
flow.say: Rub, press, try your idea, and time. Three tries for each idea. Write all the times down.
flow.kid: Test your idea three times. Write each time.

check.q: Why do we test each idea three times?
options: One try might be a fluke
Three is a lucky number
The strip gets better each time
check.why: A single try can be fast or slow for reasons that have nothing to do with your idea, such as how hard you rubbed. Three tries that agree let you trust the result.

flow.context: In this step, you test your ideas and time them.

flow.do: Look at all the times. Which idea was fastest? Change one thing about it, and test it again. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Which idea made the strip fall fastest? Why do you think it worked? What will you change next?
flow.kid: Which idea worked best? Change one thing. Test again.
flow.think: Could a printing press use your idea? What would it need?
flow.parent: Good answers say that the fast ideas gave the charge a path to the floor, or gave it a point to leak from. After they have said it, tell them that real printing presses use bars of fine metal threads, joined to the ground.
flow.context: This is the last step of the challenge. You compare your ideas and improve the best one.

items.p: A balloon is rubbed on wool and becomes charged. What actually moved?
opts: Electrons moved from the wool to the balloon
New charge was made by the rubbing
Protons moved from the wool to the balloon
items.why: Electrons are the small particles on the outside of atoms, and some can be moved. Protons are locked in the middle of the atoms and stay put. The rubbing made no new charge, it only moved some.

items.p: When a balloon is rubbed on wool, new electric charge is made.
items.why: False. Charge is never made or destroyed. Rubbing moves electrons from the wool to the balloon, so the wool loses exactly as much as the balloon gains.

items.p: A pull does not prove that a thing is charged. Only a ____ does.
items.why: A charged balloon pulls neutral things too. Only two things with the same kind of charge push each other apart, so a push is real proof.

items.p: A charged balloon swings towards a plain wooden stick. What does this show?
opts: Nothing for certain, because even neutral things are pulled
The stick is charged
The balloon has lost its charge
items.why: The balloon's charge shifts the stick's own plus and minus charges, so the nearer side has the opposite charge. That gives a small pull on a stick with no extra charge. Only a push proves that both are charged.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Conductor
lets charge move through it easily
Insulator
keeps charge where it was put
Earthing
joining a thing to the ground so charge can drain away
Polarisation
a neutral thing's charges shift when a charged thing comes near
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A conductor passes charge on and an insulator holds it. Earthing joins a thing to the ground. Polarisation is why a charged thing can pull a neutral one.

items.p: Sort each thing by what it does with a charge put on one end.
items.a: as given
items.why: Metals and salty water have charges that are free to move, so a charge spreads out and runs away. Plastic, glass and rubber hold their charges tightly, so a charge stays where it was put.

items.p: On most charge ladders, a wool shawl rubbed on polythene leaves the polythene with the minus charge.
items.why: True. Wool is near the top of the ladder and gives electrons. Polythene is near the bottom and takes them, so it ends up minus.

items.p: Put these in order on a charge ladder, from the top (gives electrons) to the bottom (takes electrons).
items.why: Hair is at the top and gives electrons to almost everything. PVC is at the bottom and takes them from almost everything. Cotton is in the middle and polyester is lower down.

items.p: Ria rubs a ruler on wool, and a hanging charged balloon swings towards the ruler. Ria says the ruler is therefore charged. Is she right? What test would settle it?
items.a: Not necessarily. A pull can happen with a neutral ruler. A push settles it: if the balloon swings away from the ruler, both have the same kind of charge.
items.why: A strong answer says that a pull is not proof, because charged things pull neutral things too, and that a push is the test.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Steel spoon, copper wire, plastic spoon, iron nail.
items.a: The plastic spoon, because it is an insulator. The other three are metals that let charge run away.
items.why: Metals are conductors, because some of their electrons are free to move. Plastic holds its electrons tightly and keeps a charge where it was put.

items.p: Why does a petrol tanker trail a metal chain or strap on the road?
opts: It lets charge from the tanker's movement drain into the ground
It makes the tanker heavier
It warns other drivers
items.why: Moving fuel and moving parts can build up charge, and a spark could set fire to the vapour. A metal strap to the ground is earthing: it gives the charge a path to drain away.

items.p: Draw a charge ladder with three rungs: wool at the top, cotton in the middle and polythene at the bottom. Draw arrows showing which way electrons go between each neighbouring pair.
items.a: A ladder with wool, cotton and polythene from top to bottom, and arrows pointing down from wool to cotton and from cotton to polythene.
items.why: Electrons go from the higher rung to the lower rung. So the arrows between each pair point down. Cotton has an arrow coming in from wool and one going out to polythene.

items.p: Charge can be moved from one thing to another, but it can never be made or ____.
items.why: This is called conservation of charge. What one thing gains, another loses, so the total stays the same.

items.p: Four tape strips are peeled apart in two pairs. Two strips are labelled T and two are labelled B. Every T pushes the other T away, and every B pushes the other B away. How many pairs of strips push each other apart?
items.why: Strips with the same kind of charge push. The two Ts make one pair and the two Bs make another pair. That is 2 pairs. The other four pairs, each with a T and a B, pull together.

items.p: Selvi and Imran have a ladder. Cotton took electrons from wool, and it gave electrons to polythene.

views.who: Selvi, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Cotton is a plus material, because it gave electrons away to polythene.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Cotton is neither one. It was minus with wool and plus with polythene, so it depends on the partner.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you say to the other?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. Imran's view fits both results, since cotton took from wool and gave to polythene.
items.why: Selvi only looked at one pair. Both results together show that cotton is minus with a partner above it and plus with a partner below it.

items.p: Clear tape is peeled off a table, and nobody rubs it, yet it ends up charged. What does this show?
opts: Touching and pulling apart is enough to move charge
Tape always carries a charge
Friction heat makes the charge
items.why: Nothing rubbed the tape, so heat from rubbing cannot be the cause. Touching and then separating two materials is enough to move electrons from one to the other. Rubbing only helps by making more of the two surfaces touch.

items.p: A bit of paper has no extra charge, yet it jumps up to a rubbed comb. Why?
opts: The comb shifts the paper's own charges, so the near side gets the opposite charge and is pulled
The paper has secretly gained a charge
The air pushes the paper up
items.why: This is polarisation. The comb's minus charge pushes the paper's electrons slightly away, so the near side of the paper is plus. A near plus side is pulled more strongly than the far minus side is pushed, so the paper rises.

items.p: A piece of cotton meets wool, and later meets polythene. Which is right?
opts: Cotton is minus with wool and plus with polythene
Cotton is plus with both
Cotton is minus with both
items.why: Wool is higher on the ladder, so it gives electrons to cotton. Polythene is lower, so cotton gives electrons to it. The cotton plays both roles.

items.p: A material can be plus with one partner and minus with another.
items.why: True. Plus and minus depend on where the two materials sit on the ladder. A material in the middle gives to those below it and takes from those above it.

items.p: If two charges are moved twice as far apart, the push between them becomes ____ as big.
items.why: The force follows the inverse square law. Twice as far means 2 times 2, which is 4, so the force is divided by 4.

items.p: Two charges 2 centimetres apart push each other with a force of 36 units. How big is the push when they are 6 centimetres apart?
items.why: 6 centimetres is 3 times as far as 2 centimetres. The force divides by 3 times 3, which is 9. 36 divided by 9 is 4 units.

items.p: Match each happening to what explains it.
pairs: A pin held near a charged balloon makes it lose its charge
A sharp point lets charge leak into the air
A tanker's trailing chain
Earthing carries charge to the ground
A paper bit jumping to a comb
Polarisation of a neutral thing
Thunder
Air heated by a spark bursting outward
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A point has a very strong field that tears charge into the air. A chain gives charge a path to the ground. A comb shifts a paper bit's charges. A spark heats air so quickly that it bursts, and we hear that as thunder.

items.p: Sort each use of static charge by whether it is used on purpose or guarded against.
items: chimney plates that catch smoke dust
items.a: as given
items.why: Printers, chimney plates and paint sprays use the push and pull of charge to put powder or droplets in the right place. Fuel, flour dust and fireworks can be set alight by one spark.

items.p: Put these in order for a lightning flash.
a: Charge separates inside the storm cloud
A faint feeler steps down from the cloud towards the ground
A bright return stroke travels up the same path
The heated air bursts outward and we hear thunder
items.why: Charge builds up first. A feeler finds a path to the ground. The bright stroke that we see goes up that path. The air it heats bursts outward with a bang.

items.p: Why can the Earth act as a bottomless drain for extra charge?
items.a: The Earth is a conductor and it is enormous, so a few billion electrons added or taken away change it by a tiny amount that nobody can measure. So charge can always run into it.
items.why: A strong answer says that the Earth conducts and is very large, so adding or taking away charge hardly changes it.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A lightning conductor's tip, a brush of thin metal threads, a pin near a charged balloon, a smooth round steel ball.
items.a: The smooth round ball, because charge spreads evenly over it. The other three are sharp points that let charge leak into the air.
items.why: Charge crowds at sharp points and the field there is strong enough to carry charge into the air. A smooth ball holds its charge more evenly.

items.p: A small spark from a door handle has about as much energy as a lightning flash.
items.why: False. The spark you feel carries a tiny amount of charge and passes in a moment. Lightning carries a huge amount of charge and has hundreds of millions of volts, so it is deadly.

items.p: Which of these do scientists still not agree about?
opts: Exactly what moves, and why, when two materials touch and part
Whether the same kinds of charge push apart
Whether charge is ever made from nothing
items.why: The other two are settled. What moves, and why one material wins over another, is still argued about. Electrons, ions and tiny bits of material have all been proposed.

items.p: A printing press has paper sheets that cling together on dry days. Two workers disagree about the best fix.

views.who: Lakshmi, a press operator (an imagined view)
views.says: Fit a bar of fine metal threads that is joined to the ground. It takes the charge off every sheet.
Keep the air in the room damp. Damp air lets charge leak away by itself.

items.ask: Whose fix would you choose? What would you want to check first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks one, gives a reason, and names a check, such as measuring if the sheets still cling after the fix. Both work, and many presses use both.
items.why: The bar gives charge a path to the ground. Damp air weakens the charge everywhere. Each has a cost, and a test shows which is better.

items.p: Draw two balloons hanging from one point after both are rubbed the same way. Show the forces on one balloon with arrows.
items.a: Two balloons hanging in a V from one point. On each balloon, an arrow down for its weight, an arrow along the thread, and an arrow pointing sideways away from the other balloon.
items.why: The sideways push comes from the other balloon's charge. Weight pulls down, and the thread pulls along its length. The balloon rests where all three balance.

items.p: Moving electrons are called minus, though the names plus and minus were chosen before electrons were found. Explain why the names stayed.
items.a: The names were a guess that happened to work in the sums. Changing them would mean changing every book and every wire, and the electron is just the thing that carries the minus charge.
items.why: A strong answer says that a name is a label that works, even if the guess behind it was backwards.

items.p: Two rubbed balloons push each other with some force at 1 centimetre apart. How strong is the push when they are 3 centimetres apart?
opts: One ninth as strong
One third as strong
The same
items.why: 3 centimetres is 3 times as far. The pull divides by 3 times 3, which is 9. That is why two balloons that push hard at 1 centimetre hardly push at 10.

items.p: A spark can jump through air when the push on the air is about ____ volts for every millimetre.
items.why: Air is an insulator until the push is strong enough. About 3,000 volts for each millimetre is where it gives way. So a 1 centimetre spark needs about 30,000 volts.

items.p: A student rubs a comb on cotton and finds that the comb pushes a charged balloon away. She says cotton must be a plus material. Why is that claim too quick?
items.a: She tested cotton against only one partner. Cotton might be plus with that comb and minus with a different partner higher up the ladder. Plus and minus belong to a pair.
items.why: A strong answer says that a result with one partner does not tell you what happens with another, because the sign depends on the pair.

items.p: Wool and nylon are close neighbours on the ladder. Why is a ladder a poor guide to rubbing them together?
opts: Their difference is so small that damp air, dirt or how hard you rub can reverse the result
Wool and nylon are both insulators
Wool and nylon have no electrons
items.why: Materials far apart give a big, steady difference. Close neighbours give a small difference, which small changes in the surface can flip. Published tables disagree about neighbours for this reason.

items.p: A balloon has taken 60,000,000,000 electrons from a woollen shawl. How many electrons has the shawl lost?
items.why: Charge is never made or destroyed. Whatever the balloon gained, the shawl lost, so the shawl lost exactly 60,000,000,000 electrons.

items.p: Two scientists argue about why rubbing moves charge between two plastics.

views.who: Dr Anwar, who studies surfaces (an imagined view)
views.says: Electrons jump from the plastic that holds them loosely to the one that holds them tightly.

views.who: Dr Beena, who studies water films (an imagined view)
views.says: Tiny films of water on every surface carry ions. The ions move, and the surface that gains them gets the charge.

items.ask: Whose idea do you find more convincing? What result could help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks one, gives a reason, and suggests a test such as repeating the rubbing in very dry air or in a vacuum, where there is no water film.
items.why: Nobody has settled it. Both ideas have evidence behind them, and good tests change one thing, such as the water, and see what stays the same.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out if damp air changes the order of materials on your ladder. Say what you would keep the same, and what you would change.
items.a: Rub the same materials, with the same number of strokes, against the same wool and polythene, and test with the same hanging balloon. Do it in dry air first, then in damp air. Only the dampness changes.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing only. The materials, the strokes, the pads and the detector must stay the same, so any difference comes from the damp air.

items.p: Why does a brush of many thin metal threads remove charge from paper better than one flat metal strip?
opts: Each thread tip is a sharp point, and charge leaks into the air easily from a point
Threads are lighter
A flat strip has no electrons
items.why: Charge crowds at points and the field there is strong enough to carry charge into the air. A hundred tips leak a lot more charge than one smooth edge.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A tanker's trailing chain, an earth pin on a plug, a pointed lightning rod, a rubber mat.
items.a: The rubber mat, because it is an insulator. The other three are conductors that carry charge to the ground.
items.why: Rubber keeps charge from moving. A chain, an earth pin and a lightning rod are metal paths that carry charge safely into the earth.

items.p: If the Earth takes a few billion electrons from you, scientists can easily measure that the Earth's charge has changed.
items.why: False. The Earth is so enormous that a few billion electrons make no difference that any instrument can find. That is why it works as a bottomless store.

items.p: The two charges made by rubbing are always equal in size and ____ in kind.
items.why: One material gains exactly the electrons the other loses. So one has extra minus, and the other has an equal shortage, which acts as plus.

items.p: Match each happening to the idea behind it.
pairs: Tape pulled off a table is charged
Touching and parting moves electrons
A pin near a charged balloon drains it
Charge leaks from a sharp point
A bee and a flower hold opposite charges
Opposite charges pull pollen across
Two rubbed balloons hang apart
Same charges repel
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each happening has a charge idea behind it. Touching and parting moves electrons. A point leaks charge. Opposite charges attract and the same repel.

items.p: Draw a bumblebee flying towards a flower. Mark the kind of charge on the bee and on the flower, and draw an arrow for the pull on a grain of pollen.
items.a: A bee marked plus and a flower marked minus, with an arrow from the pollen grain on the flower towards the bee.
items.why: A flying bee gathers a small plus charge from the air, and a flower joined to the ground is minus. Opposite charges attract, so a pollen grain can jump towards the bee.

items.p: Tape peeled from a table is charged, though nothing rubbed it. What does this say about the idea that friction heat makes the charge?
items.a: It says the idea is wrong or at least not needed. Peeling makes no friction heat, yet the tape is charged. Touching and parting is enough.
items.why: A strong answer uses the tape as evidence against the idea, since the charge appeared with no rubbing.

items.p: A neutral metal ball on a thread jumps to a charged balloon, touches it, and is then pushed away. Why is it pushed away after touching?
opts: It took some of the balloon's charge, so both have the same kind of charge now
It became heavier
The balloon lost all its charge
items.why: At first, polarisation pulls the neutral ball to the balloon. Touching lets electrons run onto the ball. Then both have minus charge, so they push apart.

items.p: The bright flash of a lightning bolt travels from the cloud down to the ground.
items.why: False. A faint feeler steps down from the cloud first. When it is near the ground, the bright return stroke travels up the same path, and that is the flash we see.

items.p: Two charges 3 centimetres apart push with a force of 18 units. What is the force when they are only 1 centimetre apart?
items.why: 1 centimetre is one third of 3 centimetres, so it is 3 times as close. The force multiplies by 3 times 3, which is 9. 18 times 9 is 162 units.

items.p: Researchers say a bumblebee senses the electric field of a flower. Some scientists want more evidence.

views.who: A researcher who studies bees (an imagined view)
views.says: The bees learned to tell flowers apart by their fields alone, so they sense them.
A bee reacting does not prove that she feels the field the way we feel touch. We need more tests.

items.ask: Whose view do you find more convincing? What further test would help?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks one, gives a reason, and suggests a test, such as hiding all other clues and seeing if the bees still choose by field.
items.why: Both views are fair. A good test removes every other clue and sees whether the bee still chooses by the field.

quiz.p: A comb rubbed on a shawl gains 5 billion electrons. How many has the shawl lost?
opts: 5 billion
10 billion
None, since charge was made
quiz.why: Charge is never made or destroyed. What one thing gains, the other loses.

quiz.p: Which result proves that a rubbed straw is charged?
opts: It pushes away a charged balloon
It picks up bits of paper
It sticks to a wall
quiz.why: Paper and walls are pulled even when they are neutral. Only a push shows that two things have the same kind of charge.

quiz.p: On a ladder, wool is rung 2 and PVC is rung 12. Wool is rubbed with PVC. Which gets the minus charge?
opts: PVC
Wool
Both get a minus
quiz.why: PVC is lower on the ladder, so it takes electrons from wool. The material that gains electrons is minus.

quiz.p: Paper is rung 5 on a ladder. It meets wool at rung 2 and PVC at rung 12. What happens?
opts: Paper is minus with wool and plus with PVC
Paper is plus with both
Paper is minus with both
quiz.why: Paper takes electrons from the rung above it, wool, and gives electrons to the rung below it, PVC. A material in the middle plays both roles.

quiz.p: Why does a charge put on a steel spoon disappear when you hold the spoon in your hand?
opts: The charge runs through the spoon and your body to the floor
Steel makes charge vanish
Steel makes new charge of the opposite kind
quiz.why: Steel and your body are both conductors. The charge spreads out and runs away to the Earth.

quiz.p: Why does touching an earthed metal pipe calm static on a sheet of paper?
opts: The pipe gives the charge a metal path to the ground
The pipe is colder than the paper
The pipe is heavier than the paper
quiz.why: An earthed pipe is joined to the ground by metal. Charge flows along it into the large Earth.

quiz.p: Two charged balloons are 4 centimetres apart. They are moved to 8 centimetres apart. What happens to the push between them?
opts: It becomes a quarter as big
It becomes half as big
It stays the same
quiz.why: The force follows the inverse square law. Twice the distance gives a quarter of the force.

quiz.p: Why do more rubs make two balloons push each other further apart?
opts: More electrons moved, so each balloon has more charge
The balloons get hotter
The wool pushes them
quiz.why: Each rub moves more electrons. More charge on each balloon means a bigger push between them.

quiz.p: What makes a spark jump across a gap of air?
opts: The push on the air gets strong enough for the air to let charge through
Air is a conductor
The air is damp
quiz.why: Air is an insulator until the push is about 3,000 volts for each millimetre. Then it gives way, and charge jumps across.

quiz.p: Which place most needs to guard against static sparks?
opts: A flour mill
A library
A bus stop
quiz.why: Fine flour dust in the air can burn very fast if a spark lights it. Mills keep the air damp and earth every metal part.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: What exactly moves, and why, when two surfaces touch and part
Whether charge is ever made from nothing
Whether the same kinds of charge push apart
quiz.why: The other two are settled. Electrons, ions and tiny pieces of material have each been proposed for the first.

quiz.p: Why does the phrase 'cotton is a plus material' mislead?
opts: Cotton is plus with some partners and minus with others
Cotton has no charge at all
Cotton is always minus
quiz.why: Plus and minus depend on the partner. Cotton gives electrons to rungs below it and takes them from rungs above it.

applications: Laser printers and photocopiers, which put black powder only where a pattern of charge has been drawn.
Chimney dust catchers in power stations, which charge the dust so it sticks to plates.
Electric paint spraying, where charged droplets push apart into a fine mist and are pulled to the object.
Earthing straps on petrol and diesel tankers, which stop charge building up near fuel vapour.
Static bars in printing and packing plants, which remove charge from paper and plastic sheets.
Lightning conductors on tall buildings, which carry a strike safely to the ground.
The earth pin on a three-pin plug, which gives stray charge a path to the ground.
Anti-static wrist straps and bags for computer chips, which stop a tiny spark from ruining them.
Air purifiers that charge dust and smoke so they stick to plates.
Flour mills and fireworks factories that keep the air damp and earth every metal part to avoid sparks.

open_questions.q: Why exactly does rubbing two materials move charge between them?
open_questions.why_open: Electrons, ions and tiny bits of material have each been seen moving in some tests and not in others. Laboratories still disagree, and it is hard to look at a surface only a few atoms thick.

open_questions.q: Why do two pieces of the very same material sometimes charge each other?
open_questions.why_open: A simple ladder cannot explain it. Research since 2011 shows patchy surfaces and size differences matter, but no one theory covers all the results.

open_questions.q: How does the very first spark of a lightning bolt start inside a storm cloud?
open_questions.why_open: The push inside a cloud seems too weak to break down air, yet lightning starts. Scientists have ideas about ice crystals and cosmic rays, and none is settled.

open_questions.q: How many animals sense electric fields, and what do they use them for?
open_questions.why_open: Bees, spiders, sharks and some fish have been studied, but most animals have not. Many studies are small and need to be repeated.

open_questions.q: Do the dust storms of the Thar desert or of Mars make lightning too?
open_questions.why_open: Rubbing grains of sand charge each other, and lightning has been seen in some dust storms on Earth. Whether it happens in every big storm, and on Mars, is not yet clear.

open_questions.q: Why are charges made only in whole units of one electron?
open_questions.why_open: Every free charge ever measured is a whole number of electron charges, but no one knows why charge comes in these units.

If you walk across a carpet in socks and touch a metal tap, what might happen? Why?
Why do you think the tape peeled off a table sticks to your hand?
Where have you seen a long metal wire running from a roof down a wall?
Why do you think a petrol pump worker sometimes touches a metal part before opening the tank?
If a thing is neutral, does that mean it has no plus and no minus? Why?
Is it easier to charge a balloon on a rainy day or a dry day? Why?
If you could only keep one rung of the charge ladder, which would you keep? Why?
What could you use at home to let the charge run out of a plastic bag that is clinging to you?
Would a bee in a storm feel different fields? What do you think?

jokes.a: It was too attached to the place.

jokes.j: What did the positive charge say to the negative charge?
Why did the electron never win an argument?
What do you call a rubbed balloon that is very sure of itself?
Why was the cotton cloth so calm?
jokes.a: It was always in the middle of things.

jokes.j: Why did the lightning conductor get promoted?
jokes.a: It was good at taking things to the ground.

jokes.j: What did one tape strip say to its twin?
jokes.a: I feel a strong pull towards you.

jokes.j: Why did the wool shawl give away its electrons?
Why did the spark cross the gap?
